extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of mythology and comparative literature
extracted.subtask_description: A chapter-length survey of major world mythic systems and their relation to English poetry, intended to help readers identify mythic themes, deity-attributes, and how mythic allusion functions in literary works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of aboriginal authenticity (Popol Vuh)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Everything relating to the Popol Vuh proves to the hilt its genuine aboriginal character; and this being so, it is of the greatest assistance to mythologists."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic, unadulterated native texts are especially valuable for comparative mythology. Note that inadequate or derivative translations reduce usefulness; the author warns that no adequate English translation yet exists and scholars must rely on Spanish and French renderings or forthcoming translations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding mythic allusions is required to appreciate myth-based poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: "Unless these allusions are understood, much of the beauty of such a work is absolutely lost."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should know the myths behind a poem (examples: Shelley's Prometheus Unbound — knowledge of characters like Panthea or Demogorgon matters). Lack of mythic knowledge will obscure references and reduce aesthetic and interpretive pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Myth as a poetical process: personification of phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: "By mythology phenomena are endowed by the barbarian mind with all the attributes of life and reason. The process is clearly a poetical one..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing myths or myth-derived poetry, treat mythic figures as poetic personifications of natural or social phenomena; look for how 'life' and agency are attributed to aspects of nature and culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary theme of early (barbarian) poetry: divine beings' stories
rubrics_metrics.description: "In a barbarian state of society the one great theme of poetry is the story of the divine beings who sway the destinies of humankind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect early epic and lyric traditions to center on gods, heroes, and cosmic events; use this as a lens when comparing poetic traditions (Pindar, Homer, Norse sagas, American Indian tribal lays are cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Myths reflect social and political structures
rubrics_metrics.description: In Greece the gods' government "appears to have been modelled upon the social polities of the various Hellenic city-states;" gods' relations mirror human institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret deity interactions, hierarchies, and conflicts as analogues of contemporary human social/political organization in the culture that produced the myths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mythology evolves with societal change
rubrics_metrics.description: As societies 'grew more enlightened' their reverence for older pantheons altered and gods' status changed (e.g., gods 'fell somewhat into disrepute').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dating or interpreting myths, account for historical social change: a deity's prominence, attributes, or reception can shift across periods and reflect cultural transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical mythic allusion as a literary resource
rubrics_metrics.description: From the Renaissance onward English poets made large use of classical and mythological allusions; such usage became a common literary ornament and model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In literary analysis, identify and contextualize classical allusions (Elizabethan to modern poets: Marlowe, Shakespeare, Spenser, Milton, Shelley, Keats, Tennyson, Morris, Swinburne). Recognize allusions function as thematic ornamentation or structural motif.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zeus–Jupiter: attributes and interpretive keys
rubrics_metrics.description: Zeus is probably originally a sky-god symbolizing the heavens, wields thunder and lightning, conquers the Titans, anthropomorphized and accumulates myths (including amorous adventures); corresponds to Roman Jupiter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When Zeus/Jupiter appears in literature, readings should consider his sky-god origins, thunder/lightning symbolism, role as chief of a pantheon, and his totemic/amorous legend accretions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apollo: solar, civilizer, and patron of arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Apollo is usually a solar deity, a civilizer or culture-hero who superintends time, protects herds, is a patron of music and poetry, and has totemic connexions (dolphin, wolf, mouse, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Apollo often signal themes of sunlight, law/order, artistic patronage, prophecy (Delphi), or cultural refinement; totemic animals can provide symbolic cues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hermes–Mercury: messenger and trickster patron
rubrics_metrics.description: Hermes is the messenger of the gods, quick-witted, ready-tongued, thievish, and traditionally patron of 'lightfingered, sharp people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appearances or allusions to Hermes suggest communication, liminality, cunning, commerce, or trickery; useful when interpreting character types or motifs involving boundary-crossing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hephaestus–Vulcan: fire, craft, and artisan-deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Hephaestus (Vulcan) is the god of fire and the great artist among the gods, maker of palaces, armour, and ingenious devices; likely evolved from an older fire/thunder deity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allusions to Hephaestus/Vulcan often index craft, technology, creation of artifacts, and the ambivalent nature of fire (destructive and domestic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hera–Juno: wife/mother archetype and patroness of marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Hera (Juno) is paramount as wife and mother, the divine prototype of the wife and mother and special patroness of marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invocations or images of Hera/Juno may foreground themes of marriage, fidelity, domestic authority, and related gender/social roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Athene–Minerva: composite war and wisdom deity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pallas Athene (Minerva) is a composite deity—storm/war goddess who also became patroness of useful crafts and abstract wisdom; emblematic animals include the owl and serpent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret Athena references as combining martial, civic, and intellectual virtues; her symbols (owl, serpent, aegis/Gorgon) signal wisdom, protection, and moral authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aphrodite–Venus: Asiatic origin and sea-foam birth motif
rubrics_metrics.description: Aphrodite (Venus) probably has Asiatic origins; mythic motifs include birth from sea-foam and a strong cultic centre in Cyprus, linking her to Astarte/Ashtaroth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Venus/Aphrodite allusions typically invoke love, beauty, fertility and may carry traces of Near Eastern associations; origin-myth variants can inform symbolic readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egyptian pantheon fluidity as interpretive factor
rubrics_metrics.description: "No definite Egyptian pantheon ever existed; as dynasties rose and fell... the deities whose cults they represented rose and fell in popularity."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using Egyptian mythic material, account for local, temporal, and dynastic variability rather than assuming a fixed hierarchy; deity prominence may reflect political/religious shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ra: solar personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Ra, the great god of the sun, is a straightforward personification of the sun and was often regarded as the greatest Egyptian god for many dynasties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ra-symbolism in texts/poetry is typically literal/solar and ties to Egyptian cosmology (daily voyage in his bark); use as a stable solar archetype in comparative readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anubis: funerary function
rubrics_metrics.description: Anubis, the jackal- or dog-headed protector of the dead, presides over the process of embalming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References to Anubis should be read in a funerary, protective, or mortuary-ritual context; his imagery signals death, preservation, and rites for the dead.
